code.highlightReason: A call through this stays on the same object, so Spring's transactional proxy cannot intercept it.
code.intro: @Transactional works at a Spring proxy boundary, not as a JVM-wide method feature.
code.takeaway: Put transactional entry points behind calls that cross a Spring-managed bean boundary.
code.title: Self-invocation skips @Transactional

hook.headline: The annotation is there. The transaction is not.
hook.hook: Spring can only apply transaction behaviour to calls it intercepts.
hook.visualCaption: A direct call on this never reaches the proxy.

interview.answer: Spring usually implements @Transactional with an AOP proxy. A call arriving through the proxy starts or joins a transaction; the proxy then commits or rolls back. A this.method() call stays inside the target object, so the annotation on the called method is not intercepted. Move that boundary to another bean or redesign the entry point.
interview.question: Why can a method annotated with @Transactional run without a transaction when called from the same class?

problems: REQUIRES_NEW, readOnly, or rollback settings can be silently ignored on self-invocation.
Objects created with new are not Spring-managed and are not transactional proxies.
production.professionalApproach: Keep transaction boundaries on public application-service methods. Extract genuinely separate transaction behaviour into another Spring bean rather than relying on self-calls.
production.scenario: An order flow should save an audit record in REQUIRES_NEW, but the audit method is called with this.recordAudit(). The audit write unexpectedly rolls back with the order.
